prompt: Why do generative AI apps and autonomous agents require security controls beyond classic application security?
choices: Prompt injection can trick them into leaking data, and oversharing exposes it
They run entirely offline, so no network control ever applies to them at all
They never process sensitive data, so no data control is needed for them
They are automatically covered by existing NSG and Azure Firewall rules already
correctAnswers: Prompt injection can trick them into leaking data, and oversharing exposes it
explanation: Both risks are invisible to classic controls: prompt injection arrives as legitimate-looking input, and oversharing means the model surfaces data the user was already technically permitted to open. The NSG option is the tempting one because those controls do exist and do apply, whereas neither of them can see a prompt or judge whether a permission was intended.

prompt: What is 'oversharing' (overexposure) in the context of Microsoft 365 Copilot?
choices: Content shared far more broadly than intended, which Copilot can then surface
A vulnerability in the weights of the underlying large language model, exploited directly
A type of prompt injection attack directed against the model
A billing overage caused by excessive AI token consumption in the tenant
correctAnswers: Content shared far more broadly than intended, which Copilot can then surface
explanation: Oversharing is a permissions problem that predates Copilot; what Copilot changes is discoverability, because it will open anything the user is permitted to open. Prompt injection is the tempting neighbour and is an attack on the model, whereas oversharing needs no attacker at all — the tenant is already misconfigured.

prompt: What does DSPM stand for in Microsoft Purview?
choices: Data Security Posture Management
Distributed Service Provisioning Model
Data Storage Protection Mechanism
Directory Security Policy Manager
correctAnswers: Data Security Posture Management
explanation: DSPM is Data Security Posture Management — Purview's discover, protect and monitor capability for sensitive data, with a dedicated view for AI. The three distractors are plausible only as expansions of the same four letters, whereas none of them names a Microsoft product: reading DSPM as anything provisioning- or directory-related puts it in the wrong portal entirely.

prompt: Which capability solves which problem? Connect each problem below to the capability that addresses it. Two of the six capabilities address none of these problems.

targets.label: Find SharePoint and OneDrive content shared far more broadly than intended, before a Copilot rollout
Detect attacks against Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI deployments while they are running
Give an AI agent a governed identity that Conditional Access and risk policies can target
Enforce Microsoft Entra authentication and token-based rate limits in front of a model endpoint

explanation: The split that matters is data-centric versus threat-centric: DSPM for AI looks at what data AI can reach, whereas Defender for AI Services looks at attacks against the AI workload itself. Confusing those two is the most common error in this objective. The two unused capabilities are real and belong elsewhere: Defender for Cloud Apps protects Copilot Studio agents at runtime, and Agent 365 is the management plane for deployed agents.

prompt: Build the 'Get started' sequence that must be completed before a Purview DSPM for AI data risk assessment can report meaningfully. Not every task in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Turn on auditing in the Microsoft Purview portal
Install the Purview browser extension in the users' browsers
Onboard the devices that will be in scope for the assessment
Run the data risk assessment against the high-risk sites
Enable the Defender for Servers Plan 2 workload protection plan
Create a Conditional Access policy scoped to agent identities
Deploy an Azure Firewall Premium instance with IDPS enabled
correctOrder: Turn on auditing in the Microsoft Purview portal
Install the Purview browser extension in the users' browsers
Onboard the devices that will be in scope for the assessment
Run the data risk assessment against the high-risk sites
explanation: The assessment reads signals it cannot produce itself, so auditing, the browser extension and device onboarding all have to be in place before it runs — an assessment executed first returns a clean report that means nothing. The three excluded tasks are tempting because each is a real security control, whereas none of them feeds Purview: two are network and server protection, and the third governs agent sign-ins rather than data discovery.

prompt: What does a DSPM for AI data risk assessment specifically look for on SharePoint/OneDrive sites?
choices: Sites or items shared far more broadly than intended
Sites consuming the most storage capacity in the tenant
Sites that are missing a retention label of any kind
Sites without a custom branding theme applied anywhere in the tenant
correctAnswers: Sites or items shared far more broadly than intended
explanation: The assessment surfaces broad sharing — "everyone except external" scopes and anonymous links — because that is what makes content reachable by Copilot on a user's behalf. The retention-label option is the tempting one since it is also a Purview finding, whereas a missing label affects how long content is kept rather than who can open it.

prompt: Which of the following is one of the DSPM for AI 'one-click' policies?
choices: Detect sensitive information pasted into AI sites
Enforce multifactor authentication for all Copilot users
Block anonymous sharing links tenant-wide
Rotate Key Vault secrets automatically
correctAnswers: Detect sensitive information pasted into AI sites
explanation: DSPM for AI's one-click policies capture Copilot prompts and responses, detect sensitive information pasted into AI sites, and detect risky AI usage. Enforcing MFA and blocking anonymous links are tempting because both are real hardening steps before a Copilot rollout, whereas they belong to Conditional Access and SharePoint sharing settings rather than to DSPM.

prompt: After enabling DSPM for AI policies, where would you review captured Copilot prompts/responses and AI usage patterns?
choices: Reports and Activity explorer ▸ AI activities
Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules
Azure Monitor Workbooks exclusively
Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard
correctAnswers: Reports and Activity explorer ▸ AI activities
explanation: DSPM for AI surfaces its findings in the Purview Reports view and Activity explorer's AI activities tab. Sentinel, Monitor Workbooks, and the compliance dashboard are not where this data-specific view lives.

prompt: Which license is required to use Purview DSPM for AI?
choices: Purview or Microsoft 365 E5
Defender for Cloud CSPM, free tier
Microsoft Entra ID P1 only
Azure Firewall Premium tier
correctAnswers: Purview or Microsoft 365 E5
explanation: DSPM for AI is a Purview capability, so it is licensed through Purview or Microsoft 365 E5 rather than through any Azure plan. The free Defender for Cloud CSPM tier is the tempting answer because posture management sounds like the same category, whereas it covers Azure resource posture and never Microsoft 365 content.

prompt: Complete the sentence that distinguishes Purview DSPM for AI from Microsoft Defender for AI Services.
template: DSPM for AI is [[b1]], while Defender for AI Services is [[b2]], raising alerts on [[b3]].

options: data-centric — it finds oversharing and sensitive data exposed to AI
threat-centric — it detects live attacks on model endpoints
network-centric — it filters traffic reaching model endpoints
identity-centric — it issues governed identities to AI agents
blanks.correctValue: data-centric — it finds oversharing and sensitive data exposed to AI

options: threat-centric — it detects attacks against AI workloads at runtime
a posture assessment run on demand against SharePoint sites
a gateway placed in front of a model endpoint
a management plane for registering deployed agents
blanks.correctValue: threat-centric — it detects attacks against AI workloads at runtime

options: Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI deployments
SharePoint sites carrying anonymous sharing links
blanks.correctValue: Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI deployments

explanation: The two are complementary and neither replaces the other: one asks what data AI can reach, the other asks who is attacking the AI. The third blank is where the products are most often confused — SharePoint oversharing is a DSPM finding, and Copilot Studio agents are covered by Defender for Cloud Apps rather than by Defender for AI Services.

prompt: What does Microsoft Entra Agent ID provide?
choices: A governed, first-class identity for AI agents that policy can target
A dedicated virtual network reserved exclusively for agent traffic only
A content filter that screens agent responses for harmful content
A billing meter that tracks the token consumption of each agent
correctAnswers: A governed, first-class identity for AI agents that policy can target
explanation: Making the agent a first-class identity is what lets Conditional Access, risk evaluation and access reviews treat it like any other principal. The content-filter option is the tempting one because it is also an AI safety control, whereas that is a Foundry guardrail and governs what the agent SAYS rather than what it may reach.

prompt: Microsoft Entra Agent ID is described as the identity foundation of which broader initiative?
choices: Microsoft Agent 365
Microsoft Defender XDR
Microsoft Purview
Azure Virtual Desktop
correctAnswers: Microsoft Agent 365
explanation: Agent 365 is the management plane for deployed agents, and Agent ID supplies the identities it registers and governs — one is the foundation of the other rather than an alternative to it. Defender XDR is the tempting answer because it is where agent incidents surface, whereas it consumes those signals instead of issuing the identity.

prompt: What is an 'agent identity' in the Entra Agent ID model?
choices: The non-human identity an agent uses to authenticate and do its work
A human administrator who manually approves every individual agent action
A network security group that is applied to all agent traffic
A Key Vault secret used exclusively for storing agent log data
correctAnswers: The non-human identity an agent uses to authenticate and do its work
explanation: The agent identity is the principal the agent authenticates as, which is what makes it governable at all. The human-approver option is tempting because approval gates do exist around agents, whereas those are policies applied TO the identity rather than the identity itself — and an agent that needed a human for every action would not be autonomous.

prompt: What is an agent's 'user account' used for?
choices: Giving the agent a mailbox and group memberships as a digital colleague
Storing the model weights and training data belonging to the agent
Encrypting the prompt and response logs that the agent produces
Defining which Conditional Access policies are excluded from being evaluated
correctAnswers: Giving the agent a mailbox and group memberships as a digital colleague
explanation: The user account exists so an agent can hold the things a colleague holds — a mailbox, group memberships, a place in a workflow. The Conditional Access option is the trap and inverts the relationship: the linked user account is a SEPARATE policy scope that must be configured on its own, rather than an exclusion from policy.

prompt: What is an 'agent identity blueprint'?
choices: A template that creates agent identities consistently and holds no access
A signed container image used to run the agent runtime in production clusters
A category of recommendation raised by Microsoft Defender for Cloud
A Key Vault access policy template that is applied to stored secrets
correctAnswers: A template that creates agent identities consistently and holds no access
explanation: A blueprint is a factory, not a principal: it produces identities with a consistent shape and can itself reach nothing, which is why granting it access is meaningless. The container-image option is tempting because both are called templates in ordinary use, whereas one describes what the agent RUNS and the other what it IS.

prompt: How can custom security attributes be used with AI agents?
choices: Labels that Conditional Access policies can target to scope rules
Encryption keys that protect the secrets an agent holds in Key Vault
DNS labels used by private endpoints carrying agent traffic
Custom RBAC role definitions granted directly to an agent identity
correctAnswers: Labels that Conditional Access policies can target to scope rules
explanation: An attribute such as AgentApprovalStatus=IT_Approved lets one policy cover every approved agent automatically, so no policy has to be edited when an agent is added. The custom RBAC option is the tempting one because both are ways of describing what an agent may do, whereas a role grants permissions directly and an attribute only describes the agent so a policy can find it.

prompt: In the Entra admin center, which Conditional Access assignment type targets AI agent identities?
choices: Agents (Preview), the workload identity type
Named locations, defined by trusted IP ranges
Directory roles currently held in the tenant
Terms of use acceptance records
correctAnswers: Agents (Preview), the workload identity type
explanation: Agents are assigned as a workload identity type, which is why the policy can never be found under Users. Named locations is the tempting pick because it appears on the same policy blade, whereas it is a CONDITION describing where a sign-in comes from rather than an assignment naming who the policy is about.

prompt: Which Conditional Access condition can automatically flag and gate a risky AI agent?
choices: Agent risk (Preview) set to High
Sign-in risk set to Medium
Device compliance = Noncompliant
Client app = Legacy authentication
correctAnswers: Agent risk (Preview) set to High
explanation: Agent risk is the condition scoped to agent identities, so a high-risk agent is gated with no human in the loop. Sign-in risk is the closest miss and evaluates a user authentication attempt, whereas device compliance cannot apply at all — an agent has no device to be compliant.

prompt: What is the recommended rollout approach for a new Conditional Access policy targeting agents?
choices: Start in Report-only mode, validate the impact, then switch to enforce
Enable Block access in production immediately, with no testing whatsoever
Skip testing entirely, since agent sign-ins are not logged anywhere
Apply the policy to the break-glass accounts first, and only those
correctAnswers: Start in Report-only mode, validate the impact, then switch to enforce
explanation: Report-only evaluates the policy against real sign-ins and records what it would have done, which is how an over-broad agent policy is caught before it stops a production workflow. The break-glass option is the tempting inversion: those accounts are the ones to EXCLUDE from a policy, never the pilot group to test it on.

prompt: For each statement about Conditional Access and AI agents, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: A policy targeting an agent identity also covers sign-ins by the agent's linked user account.
Agent risk is available as a Conditional Access condition, so a high-risk agent can be gated automatically.
When an agent calls a backend API with a raw API key, Conditional Access still evaluates the call.
A policy left in Report-only mode logs what it would have done without blocking anything.

explanation: The two false statements are the two ways agent coverage is over-estimated. The agent identity and its linked user account are separate scopes, so a policy on one does not reach the other. And a raw API key bypasses Entra ID entirely — no token is requested, so there is no sign-in for Conditional Access to evaluate, which is why an AI gateway enforcing Entra authentication is what closes that path.

prompt: An agent calls a backend API using a raw API key instead of Microsoft Entra authentication. What is the security implication?
choices: Conditional Access does not apply, because the key path bypasses Entra
Conditional Access still fully applies, because the agent has an Entra identity
The API key is rotated and secured automatically by Microsoft Entra ID
Microsoft Defender for AI Services blocks the call automatically in all cases
correctAnswers: Conditional Access does not apply, because the key path bypasses Entra
explanation: Conditional Access evaluates token issuance, so a call that never asks Entra for a token is never evaluated — having an Entra identity is not the same as using it. That is the tempting answer here, and it is why the remedy is architectural: put an AI gateway in front of the endpoint so Entra authentication is the only accepted path.

prompt: What is the recommended alternative to API keys for securing agent-to-API calls?
choices: Microsoft Entra ID-based authentication
Basic authentication with a shared password
A static bearer token embedded in the agent's source code
IP allow-listing as the sole control
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra ID-based authentication
explanation: Using Entra-based auth keeps the call inside Entra's governance, so Conditional Access and risk policies actually apply. Shared passwords, embedded static tokens, and IP allow-listing alone don't provide identity-based governance.

prompt: After Entra flags an agent as high-risk, which tool should you use to assess its blast radius (what resources/data/identities it could reach)?
choices: Microsoft Defender XDR
Purview Compliance Manager
Azure Cost Management
Azure Advisor recommendations
correctAnswers: Microsoft Defender XDR
explanation: Defender XDR correlates the agent with the identities, devices and data it touched, which is what a blast-radius question actually asks. Compliance Manager is the tempting neighbour because it is also an assessment tool, whereas it scores your control posture against a regulation rather than tracing one identity's reach.

prompt: Which service manages the ongoing lifecycle (review, approve, remove) of an agent's access?
choices: Microsoft Entra ID Governance with Agent 365
Microsoft Sentinel automation rules and playbooks
Azure Policy assignments at scope
Azure Backup with recovery vaults
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra ID Governance with Agent 365
explanation: Access reviews, approval workflows and removal are ID Governance functions, and Agent 365 is where they are exercised for agents specifically. Sentinel playbooks are the tempting answer because automation sounds like lifecycle management, whereas a playbook reacts to an incident rather than periodically recertifying whether access is still needed.

prompt: What does Microsoft Defender for AI Services monitor?
choices: Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI deployments, for AI-specific threats
On-premises file shares only, scanning each of them for malware signatures
Network traffic passing between two peered virtual networks
Azure DevOps pipeline definitions and their service connections
correctAnswers: Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI deployments, for AI-specific threats
explanation: The plan watches the model-serving resources themselves and raises AI-specific alerts such as jailbreak attempts and wallet attacks. Each distractor names a real Defender or Azure capability, which is what makes the list plausible, whereas none of them is scoped to an AI workload.

prompt: Which underlying capability powers Defender for AI Services' detection of jailbreak and prompt injection attempts?
choices: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields
Azure Firewall Premium IDPS signatures
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint EDR sensors
Azure DDoS Protection Standard
correctAnswers: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields
explanation: Prompt Shields, part of Azure AI Content Safety, is the underlying technology that detects jailbreak and injection attempts feeding Defender for AI Services alerts. Firewall IDPS, EDR sensors, and DDoS Protection target network- or endpoint-layer threats, not model prompts.

prompt: What does a 'wallet attack' alert in Defender for AI Services indicate?
choices: Abuse designed to drive up cost by forcing excessive model usage
A stolen Key Vault secret being used to reach a storage account
A phishing campaign aimed specifically at the finance department
A denial-of-service attack directed at a storage account endpoint
correctAnswers: Abuse designed to drive up cost by forcing excessive model usage
explanation: The target is the bill rather than the data: an attacker drives token consumption until the cost becomes the damage. The finance-phishing option is tempting because of the word wallet, whereas the attack has nothing to do with people or payments — which is why the defence is a token-based rate limit at the gateway.

prompt: Where do you enable the Defender for AI Services plan?
choices: Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Defender plans
Entra admin center ▸ Protection ▸ Conditional Access ▸ Policies
Microsoft Purview portal ▸ DSPM for AI ▸ Recommendations
Azure API Management ▸ Products ▸ Policies
correctAnswers: Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Defender plans
explanation: Every Defender plan is switched on per environment under Environment settings, which is the one location worth memorising because it is the same for Storage, Servers and AI Services alike. The Purview route is the tempting miss and leads to the data-centric product instead — different portal, different question.

prompt: Each row below describes one object in the Entra Agent ID model. Identify it. Two entries in the list describe no row.

targets.label: The non-human identity the agent authenticates and acts as
Gives the agent a mailbox and group memberships, as a digital colleague
A template that creates agent identities consistently and can itself reach nothing
A label such as AgentApprovalStatus=IT_Approved that a Conditional Access policy can target

explanation: The blueprint is the one most often misread as a principal: it produces identities and holds no access of its own, whereas the agent identity is what actually authenticates. The two unused entries are ordinary Azure VM controls with no place in the agent identity model, and both are tempting only because they are familiar Azure nouns.

prompt: Which two capabilities are part of Microsoft Foundry guardrails? (Choose two.)
choices: Prompt Shields, which block jailbreak and injection attempts
Content filters with severity thresholds for harmful categories
Azure Disk Encryption applied to the VM volumes hosting the model
Network security group rules applied to the model subnet
correctAnswers: Prompt Shields, which block jailbreak and injection attempts
Content filters with severity thresholds for harmful categories
explanation: Guardrails act on the content flowing through the model — what comes in, and what goes out. The two distractors are genuine Azure controls protecting the infrastructure the model runs on, which is a different layer: neither can see a prompt, whereas neither guardrail protects a disk.

prompt: Which two benefits does placing Azure API Management in front of model endpoints (as an AI gateway) provide? (Choose two.)
choices: Microsoft Entra ID authentication instead of raw API keys
Token-based rate limiting that defends against wallet attacks
Automatic fine-tuning of the underlying model on the request data
Encryption at host for the virtual machines hosting the model
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra ID authentication instead of raw API keys
Token-based rate limiting that defends against wallet attacks
explanation: The gateway changes how the endpoint is reached: Entra authentication brings Conditional Access back into a path an API key would have bypassed, and a token quota caps the cost an attacker can inflict. Fine-tuning is the tempting distractor because it is a real model operation, whereas a gateway never modifies the model.

prompt: Referring to requirement 1 (find SharePoint sites shared far too broadly before enabling Copilot tenant-wide), which action should the security team take first?
choices: Run a Purview DSPM for AI data risk assessment on high-risk sites
Enable Microsoft Defender for AI Services on the Foundry resource
Create a Conditional Access policy blocking any high-risk agent
Disable the admin account on the Azure Container Registry instance
correctAnswers: Run a Purview DSPM for AI data risk assessment on high-risk sites
explanation: The requirement is about data exposure before rollout, which is exactly what the DSPM assessment reports. Defender for AI Services is the tempting alternative because it is the other AI security product, whereas it watches for attacks on the Foundry workload and would report nothing at all about SharePoint sharing.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (the new Foundry-based support agent needs a governed, first-class identity so Conditional Access and risk-based policies apply to it like a human user), which configuration meets this requirement?
choices: Provision the agent with a Microsoft Entra Agent ID identity
Give the agent a shared service account password used across every agent
Grant the agent Global Administrator so it is never inadvertently blocked
Rely solely on the agent's API key rotation schedule for governance
correctAnswers: Provision the agent with a Microsoft Entra Agent ID identity
explanation: An Entra Agent ID identity is the governed, first-class identity that lets Conditional Access and Identity Protection risk apply to the agent as they would to a person. Granting Global Administrator so the agent is never blocked is the tempting shortcut and is the opposite of the requirement: it removes the governance being asked for rather than supplying it.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (the agent must be blocked automatically if Microsoft Entra flags it as high-risk, without a human needing to notice first), which configuration is correct?
choices: An enforced CA policy on the agent identity: Agent risk High, Block access
A daily manual review of Microsoft Defender XDR incidents by the SOC team on rotation
A Report-only Conditional Access policy that only logs matching sign-ins
An Azure Policy Audit effect applied to the Foundry resource in scope
correctAnswers: An enforced CA policy on the agent identity: Agent risk High, Block access
explanation: The words "automatically" and "without a human noticing" rule out three of the four options at once. Report-only is the closest miss and is otherwise the right policy — it simply does not block, so it satisfies the detection half and fails the enforcement half, which is the distinction the requirement is built around.

prompt: Referring to requirement 4 (model endpoints behind the support agent must enforce Microsoft Entra authentication instead of API keys, and apply token-based rate limits against wallet attacks), which configuration is correct?
choices: Azure API Management as an AI gateway, with Entra auth and token limits
Enable Azure Disk Encryption on the compute hosting the Foundry deployment
Rotate the model endpoint's API keys on a weekly schedule instead
Add an NSG rule restricting the model endpoint to a single subnet
correctAnswers: Azure API Management as an AI gateway, with Entra auth and token limits
explanation: Both halves of the requirement are gateway functions, and only a gateway can enforce them at the endpoint. Weekly key rotation is the tempting compromise because it does reduce the window of a leaked key, whereas the requirement is to stop using keys at all — rotation keeps the path that bypasses Conditional Access.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable Microsoft 365 Copilot tenant-wide first, then review Copilot usage reports weekly to spot oversharing after the fact. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: The goal is to find oversharing BEFORE the rollout, and reviewing usage reports weekly only reveals it after Copilot has already surfaced the content to the wrong people. The solution is tempting because the reports genuinely do show the exposure, whereas by then the disclosure has happened and cannot be undone.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable Microsoft Defender for AI Services on the Azure OpenAI resource before the Copilot rollout. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Defender for AI Services detects threats against Foundry/Azure OpenAI deployments (jailbreak, data leakage, wallet attacks) — it does not discover SharePoint/OneDrive oversharing, so it does not meet this specific goal.

prompt: Proposed solution: Run a Purview DSPM for AI data risk assessment against SharePoint sites before enabling Copilot tenant-wide, and remediate any flagged overexposed sites. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: This is the intended workflow: the assessment discovers broad sharing, remediation fixes it, and only then does Copilot get the chance to surface anything. Note the prerequisite it assumes rather than states — auditing, the browser extension and device onboarding must already be in place, otherwise the assessment reports a clean tenant it never actually inspected.

prompt: Order the steps to evaluate AI data risk with Purview DSPM for AI in a fresh tenant.
reorderItems: Open the Purview portal ▸ Solutions ▸ DSPM for AI
Complete the Get started tasks: enable Audit, install the browser extension, and onboard devices
Run a data risk assessment against high-risk SharePoint sites
Turn on one-click policies (prompt capture, sensitive-info detection, risky AI usage)
Review findings in Reports and Activity explorer ▸ AI activities
explanation: The Get started prerequisites come before the assessment, the one-click policies before the reports, and the review last. Running the assessment first is the ordering mistake that matters most, because it does not fail — it returns findings from signals that were never collected, which reads as a clean tenant rather than an incomplete scan.

prompt: Order the steps to create a Conditional Access policy that automatically blocks high-risk AI agents.
reorderItems: Sign in to the Entra admin center ▸ Conditional Access ▸ Policies ▸ New policy
Under Assignments, target Agents (Preview) — include all agent identities or scope by custom security attribute
Set Target resources to All resources and the condition Agent risk (Preview) to High
Under Grant, select Block access, and enable the policy in Report-only mode
Review the Report-only results, then switch the policy to On to enforce
explanation: Assignment and resource scope first, then the Agent risk condition, then the Block grant, and Report-only before enforcement. Switching straight to On is the ordering mistake, and its consequence is specific to agents rather than to people: an over-broad block stops an automated workflow with no human present to notice it has stopped.

prompt: Configure this simplified Conditional Access screen so a high-risk AI agent identity is blocked automatically, without requiring a human to notice first.
explanation: Targeting all agent identities, setting Agent risk to High, granting Block access, and enforcing (not Report-only) together produce an automatic block with no human intervention required — matching the stated requirement.

prompt: Which capability provides real-time runtime protection specifically for agents built in Copilot Studio, surfacing their inventory and alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Settings for AI
Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI, risk assessments view
Microsoft Defender for AI Services threat plan
Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity blueprints
correctAnswers: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Settings for AI
explanation: Copilot Studio agents are covered by Defender for Cloud Apps, which is the answer most people miss because the name says nothing about AI. Defender for AI Services is the tempting pick and covers Foundry and Azure OpenAI instead — same Defender family, different workload, and choosing by name rather than by workload is the error.

prompt: You enable Copilot Studio agent protection in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, but no agents appear in Defender XDR's Advanced Hunting data. What is the most likely missing step?
choices: Coordinating with Power Platform admins to configure the agent's App ID
Adding a Conditional Access policy for the agent's linked user account first
Enabling Microsoft Entra ID P2 licensing across the tenant
Disabling Shared Key authorization on the storage account
correctAnswers: Coordinating with Power Platform admins to configure the agent's App ID
explanation: Copilot Studio agents live in Power Platform, so the App ID has to be configured there before Defender can associate telemetry with an agent — which makes this a cross-team dependency rather than a Defender setting. The Conditional Access option is tempting because it also concerns the agent, whereas a policy governs sign-ins and would not create a single hunting record.

prompt: Which product provides the management plane to register deployed AI agents, apply access controls, and monitor agent usage to enforce organizational AI governance policies across Microsoft 365?
choices: Microsoft Agent 365
Microsoft Entra Agent ID
Microsoft Foundry
Azure API Management
correctAnswers: Microsoft Agent 365
explanation: Microsoft Agent 365 is the governance and lifecycle management plane for deployed agents — registering them, applying access controls, and monitoring usage. Entra Agent ID is the identity layer agents authenticate with, not the governance plane.

prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish Microsoft Entra Agent ID from Microsoft Agent 365? (Choose two.)
choices: Entra Agent ID provides the non-human identity an agent acts as
Agent 365 is the management plane for registering and monitoring agents
They are simply two marketing names for the exact same single product
Agent 365 removes any need to configure Entra Agent ID at all, in any tenant
correctAnswers: Entra Agent ID provides the non-human identity an agent acts as
Agent 365 is the management plane for registering and monitoring agents
explanation: One issues the identity, the other manages the fleet — they are layers of the same story rather than competitors. Both false statements make the same mistake from opposite directions: they collapse the two into one product, whereas Agent 365 depends on Agent ID and cannot replace it.

prompt: Which Defender for Cloud capability combines CSPM posture findings and Defender for AI Services runtime alerts specifically for AI resources behind a single enablement toggle, with combined insights in the Data and AI security dashboard?
choices: The AI workloads plan in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Policy regulatory compliance initiatives, assigned
Microsoft Defender for Storage, malware scanning
Microsoft Sentinel automation rules and playbooks
correctAnswers: The AI workloads plan in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
explanation: The AI workloads plan is the single toggle that brings posture and runtime findings for AI resources together on one dashboard. Azure Policy regulatory compliance is the tempting neighbour because it also aggregates posture, whereas it reports configuration against a standard and carries no runtime alerts at all.

prompt: Order the steps to enable and verify runtime protection for a Copilot Studio agent end to end.
reorderItems: Enable the AI protection setting in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
Coordinate with Power Platform admins to configure the agent's App ID
Confirm the agent appears in the Defender XDR agent inventory
Review alerts and Advanced Hunting data for the agent in Defender XDR
explanation: Protection is enabled in Defender for Cloud Apps first, but nothing appears until Power Platform admins configure the App ID — which is why the inventory check belongs before the hunting step rather than after it. Expecting telemetry straight after enabling the setting is the assumption that makes this look broken when it is merely incomplete.

prompt: Across the tenant, business users have published dozens of Copilot agents. An administrator must see the full inventory, review who published each one, and block a specific agent from being used. Where is that agent lifecycle managed?
choices: The Microsoft 365 admin center, which holds the tenant-wide agent inventory and the controls to review and block individual agents
Microsoft Defender for Cloud, on the Data and AI security dashboard alongside the other AI posture and alert findings for the tenant
Microsoft Foundry, in the guardrails configuration where content filters and Prompt Shields are defined
Microsoft Entra, under the Agent ID blade where each agent's directory identity and its access are managed
correctAnswers: The Microsoft 365 admin center, which holds the tenant-wide agent inventory and the controls to review and block individual agents
explanation: Agent lifecycle — inventory, publisher, and availability — is a Microsoft 365 admin center task, and this portal split is itself examinable. The Entra Agent ID blade is the closest miss: it governs an agent's identity and what that identity may reach, not whether the agent is published to users. Defender for Cloud reports posture and Foundry constrains model behaviour; neither one lists or blocks a published agent.

prompt: An agent with a Microsoft Entra Agent ID is suspected of being compromised. Before deciding whether to revoke its access, the security team must establish what the agent could have reached. Which Defender XDR capability answers that question?
choices: Blast radius analysis for the agent identity, which enumerates the resources and data that identity can reach
Advanced hunting over the agent's sign-in table, which lists every resource that identity has actually authenticated to
The Data and AI security dashboard in Defender for Cloud, which scores the tenant's overall AI posture
A Conditional Access policy in report-only mode, which logs what the agent would have been allowed to do
correctAnswers: Blast radius analysis for the agent identity, which enumerates the resources and data that identity can reach
explanation: Blast radius is a question about potential impact, not about history, and that distinction is the item. Hunting the sign-in records tells you where the agent has already been, which understates the exposure — anything it had permission to open but never opened is missed. The dashboard reports posture at tenant level rather than for one identity, and report-only Conditional Access is a rollout technique for a policy that does not exist yet.

prompt: An incident involves a Microsoft Entra Agent ID. For each of the following statements about assessing and containing it, select Yes if the statement is true, or No if it is not.

statements.text: Blast radius analysis reports what the agent identity is permitted to reach, not only what it has already accessed.
Because agents hold first-class directory identities, their access can be revoked the same way a user's is.
Removing the agent from the Microsoft 365 admin center inventory also strips the permissions its Agent ID holds.
An agent running on a shared service principal has a smaller blast radius than one with its own Agent ID.

explanation: Agent ID exists so that an agent is governable like any other principal — inventoried, assessed, revoked. The two No rows are the misconceptions worth breaking. Blocking an agent in the admin center stops it being offered to users but leaves its identity and grants intact, so containment needs both surfaces. And a shared service principal is strictly worse, not better: every agent on it inherits the union of the permissions, so the blast radius grows with each one added.

correctAnswers: The Data and AI security dashboard, which consolidates AI workload inventory, exposure and alerts
explanation: Each surface answers a different question and the portal split is examinable. The dashboard is the cross-subscription posture and alerting view, which is what a tenant-wide picture requires. Purview DSPM for AI is the tempting alternative because it also reports on AI risk, but its subject is the data users can reach rather than the workloads themselves. The admin center covers agent lifecycle and Foundry covers model-side controls; neither aggregates alerts.

Getting this wrong is the most common AI-security mistake on this objective, because every surface plausibly relates to AI. Entra Agent ID and the API Management gateway are the sharpest distractors: both are real AI controls, but one governs an agent's identity and the other the traffic to a model endpoint, and neither answers any of the four questions above.
